rationale: A wins because it keeps the tension inside the facts and shows the holes instead of decorating them. Its best line, "A Calm-funded trial reports an 18% drop in anxiety — the question is whether \"regular users\" is doing the heavy lifting," is exactly the kind of skeptical-but-fair framing a science reporter can use. B has useful bones, but "Are health insurers using a meditation app instead of paying for real anxiety care?" jumps from covered benefit to implied care substitution without evidence; that's not edge, that's a legal review waiting to happen.
gaps_in_A: "once growth slows" sneaks in market context not present in the update; keep it as a reporter beat, not an implied Calm condition.
"evidentiary spine of the insurer deal" implies the study supports the payer deal; the facts only say the deal and study are being announced/published together.

"Wellness apps are crossing from app-store impulse buy into reimbursed health benefit" is broader than one Calm deal can prove; A correctly asks for comparable cases, but the headline should carry that caution.
gaps_in_B: "Are health insurers using a meditation app instead of paying for real anxiety care?" is a serious substitution claim with no evidence that therapy or psychiatry coverage changed.
"default benefit for 25 million Americans" overstates the facts; the update says a no-cost covered benefit for an estimated 25 million members, not default usage or Americans.
"perk" to standard coverage turns one insurer partnership into a settled trend without comparable deals or plan-design evidence.
"cut other mental-health benefits" is an invented risk framed as something to check; fine as an internal question, too loaded as a pitch premise.
